title: The Call of Abram and a Detour into Egypt
summary: The LORD calls Abram to leave his country and family for a land he will be shown, promising to make him a great nation, to bless him, to make his name great, and to bless all the families of the earth through him. Abram obeys at seventy-five, travels through Canaan, and builds altars at Shechem and near Bethel after God promises the land to his offspring. When famine strikes he goes down to Egypt, where fear leads him to pass Sarai off as his sister; she is taken into Pharaoh's palace until the LORD strikes Pharaoh's house with plagues, and Pharaoh sends Abram away.
story:
This is the hinge of Genesis and, in a real sense, of the whole Bible. Chapters 1 to 11 told the story of all humanity and ended with sin spreading, curse multiplying, and the nations scattered after Babel, where the builders tried to make a name for themselves (11:4). Now God answers the whole world's problem by speaking to one man, and he promises to make that man's name great himself. The promises of verses 1 to 3 set the agenda for everything that follows: offspring, land, and blessing for the nations. Israel's history, the kingdom of David, the prophets' hopes, and the mission of the church all trace back to this call.

The call comes to a family already marked by loss. Sarai is barren (11:30), Abram's brother Haran has died in Ur (11:28), and Terah's household had set out for Canaan but stopped at Haran (11:31). The chapter belongs to the section Genesis heads ‘the account of Terah’ (11:27), and Abram now finishes the trip his father began. Yet the chapter does not end in triumph. Within a few verses the man of promise is in Egypt, lying to protect himself and endangering the very wife through whom the promised offspring must come. God's promise, not Abram's character, carries the story forward, and the pattern of famine, descent to Egypt, plagues, and departure with wealth sketches in advance the story of the exodus.
historical:
The stories of Abram have traditionally been placed in the early second millennium BC. A straightforward addition of the Bible's own numbers (the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1, the 430 years of Exodus 12:40, and the patriarchs' ages) puts his departure from Haran a little before 2000 BC, though each link in that chain is debated, and the date of the exodus itself is contested. Many critical scholars, following Thomas L. Thompson (The Historicity of the Patriarchal Narratives, 1974) and John Van Seters (Abraham in History and Tradition, 1975), regard the patriarchal stories as compositions of the first millennium that cannot be dated to any historical period; others, such as Kenneth Kitchen (On the Reliability of the Old Testament, 2003), argue that many details fit the second millennium better than any later age. The introduction to Genesis sets out these positions.

Haran, where the call finds Abram (verse 4; Acts 7:2-4 places a first call earlier, in Ur), was a real and important city on the Balikh River in upper Mesopotamia, in what is now southeastern Turkey. Like Ur in the south, it was a center of the worship of the moon god Sin, and Mesopotamian kings from the second millennium to Nabonidus in the sixth century BC rebuilt its moon temple, the Ehulhul. Joshua 24:2 remembers that Terah's family ‘worshiped other gods’ beyond the Euphrates. The names of Abram's relatives match towns of the Haran region known from cuneiform texts: Nahur (Nahor), Sarugi (Serug), and Til-Turahi (Terah).

Canaan in the Middle Bronze Age was a land of walled city-states. Shechem (Tell Balata) is the first Canaanite town named in an Egyptian text: the stela of Khu-Sebek, an officer of Senusret III (nineteenth century BC), records a campaign against Sekmem, and the Egyptian Execration Texts of the same period, curses written on figurines and bowls, name a ruler of Shechem. Bethel and Ai lay about twenty kilometers north of Jerusalem, and the Negev, the dry grazing land around Beersheba, was the first region to feel a failure of the winter rains.

When rain failed in Canaan, Egypt, watered by the Nile's yearly flood, was the natural place to find food. A painting in the tomb of the provincial governor Khnumhotep II at Beni Hasan, dated to the sixth year of Senusret II (about 1890 BC), shows thirty-seven brightly dressed Aamu, people from western Asia, arriving in Egypt with donkeys, women, and children under a leader named Abisha. Much later, Papyrus Anastasi VI (late thirteenth century BC) records a frontier official letting herdsmen from Edom pass a border fort to keep their flocks alive.

The king of Egypt is called Pharaoh, from the Egyptian per-aa, great house. In the Old and Middle Kingdoms the phrase meant the palace; in the Eighteenth Dynasty (from the fifteenth century BC) it came to be used for the king himself, and only in the first millennium did Egyptians attach it to a king's personal name, which is how the books of Kings later speak of Pharaoh Neco (2 Kings 23:29). Genesis never names its Pharaoh.

The camels of verse 16 have been debated. Lidar Sapir-Hen and Erez Ben-Yosef, dating camel bones from copper-mining sites in the Aravah Valley (Tel Aviv 40, 2013, widely reported in 2014), found that domesticated camels appear in the southern Levant in large numbers only in the last third of the tenth century BC. Some scholars therefore take the reference as a detail from the narrator's own day; others answer that the study measures when camels became common as pack animals in that valley, and that small numbers of camels are known in Egypt and Mesopotamia earlier.
cultural:
Leaving one's country, kindred, and father's household was a staggering request in the ancient world. The father's house (bet av) was the basic unit of Israelite and Near Eastern society: it held the land, the flocks, the family gods and graves, and the name that would be remembered. A man without it had no protector, no inheritance, and no one to avenge him. To leave it was to become a ger, a resident alien who lived by the goodwill of the people whose land it was. Abram does exactly that, and the chapter shows him living as an outsider in a land already occupied, with a tent for himself and altars for God.

The places Abram visits were sacred sites. The Oak of Moreh (verse 6) takes its name from a word related to the verb for teaching or giving direction, and a tree near Shechem called the Diviners' Oak appears in Judges 9:37; great trees were places where people sought oracles, which is why the prophets later condemned worship ‘under every green tree’. Shechem became the place where Jacob buried his household's idols under the oak (35:4) and where Joshua renewed the covenant under a great tree (Joshua 24:26). Bethel became a royal sanctuary of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 12:29). By building altars there, Abram marks the land as belonging to the LORD before any Israelite owns a field in it. ‘Calling on the name of the LORD’ (verse 8) repeats 4:26 and describes worship addressed to God by his name.

The episode in Egypt reflects the vulnerability of a foreigner with a beautiful wife. Abram fears that powerful men will kill him to take her; a husband stood in the way, a brother could be bargained with. Sarai was in fact his half-sister, the daughter of his father but not of his mother (20:12), a marriage the later law would forbid (Leviticus 18:9), so his words were a half-truth designed to deceive. Kings took women of beauty or diplomatic value into their households, and Pharaoh's gifts of flocks, donkeys, servants, and camels look like a lavish bride-price paid to the woman's brother (compare 34:12). Abram leaves Egypt wealthy, and the maidservants he gained may include Hagar the Egyptian (16:1), whose presence will bring its own trouble. His wealth was gained at his wife's expense.

The mid-twentieth century saw a famous attempt to explain the ‘wife-sister’ stories from ancient law. E. A. Speiser (1963, and in his Anchor Bible Genesis, 1964) argued that tablets from Nuzi, a Hurrian town in northern Mesopotamia, show a legal institution in which a wife could also be adopted as her husband's sister, giving her higher status, and that Genesis preserves a garbled memory of it. Samuel Greengus (Hebrew Union College Annual 46, 1975) showed that the Nuzi texts do not support this reading, and the theory is now generally abandoned. The story makes sense on its own terms: it is about fear, not a legal fiction.
literary:
The chapter has two parts that sit in sharp tension. Verses 1 to 9 present Abram at his best: God speaks, and Abram goes, without a word of reply. The narrator reports his obedience in the very words of the command (verse 4 answers lekh, go, with vayyelekh, he went) and adds the phrase ‘as the LORD had directed him’, the formula used for Noah's obedience (6:22). Verses 10 to 20 then show Abram at his weakest. In the first half he never speaks; in the second he makes the chapter's only human speech, a plan for his own safety, and when Pharaoh confronts him he is silent again. Sarai never speaks at all, and the verbs used of her are passive: she is seen, praised, and taken.

The promise in verses 2 and 3 uses the root for blessing five times, answering the five times the verb for cursing (arar) has appeared in the chapters before (3:14, 3:17, 4:11, 5:29, and 9:25). It also answers Babel. The builders of 11:4 wanted to make a name and feared being scattered; God promises Abram a great name and sends him out, and the scattered ‘families’ of the table of nations in chapter 10 (the same word, mishpachot) are named as the ones to be blessed. The promise has two movements, each with first-person verbs of God's resolve followed by a result: God will make, bless, and make great, so that Abram will be a blessing (verse 2); God will bless and curse, so that all families will find blessing (verse 3).

The command go (lekh-lekha) is heard in Abraham's story only one other time, in 22:2, when God tells him to go to the land of Moriah, to a mountain God will show him. The two calls frame Abraham's story: the first cuts him off from his past, the second seems to cut him off from his future. The Egypt episode is the first of three ‘wife-sister’ stories (12:10-20, 20:1-18, 26:6-11). Hermann Gunkel's commentary (1901) treated them as variants of one folk tale; later literary readers, such as Robert Alter (The Art of Biblical Narrative, 1981), read such repetitions as deliberate type-scenes whose differences carry meaning. Here the episode previews the exodus: famine drives the family down to Egypt, Pharaoh takes what is not his, the LORD strikes him with plagues (nega, the word of Exodus 11:1), and Pharaoh sends them away (shillach, the verb of ‘let My people go’) with great possessions. Pharaoh's question, “What have you done to me?” (verse 18), echoes God's question to the woman in 3:13, but now a pagan king is rebuking the man of promise.

outline.t: Abram obeys and comes to Canaan
The promise of the land and altars at Shechem and Bethel
The LORD's plagues and Pharaoh's rebuke

doctrines.note: Abram's first response to God is simply to go, leaving everything familiar for a land he has not seen, on the strength of God's word (verse 4). Faith here is obedience to a promise, not a feeling. Yet the same chapter shows faith failing under pressure, as fear leads Abram to deceive (verses 11 to 13). Faith in Scripture is real and imperfect at once, and Hebrews 11:8 remembers the going, not the lapse.

Though the word covenant does not appear until chapter 15, God's promises here are its foundation: a great nation, a great name, a land for his offspring (verse 7), and blessing. They are given before Abram has done anything, as God's own commitments, and the rest of Genesis traces how he keeps them through generations of failure.

God's choice of Abram is not favoritism but strategy. He blesses one family so that all the families of the earth will be blessed through him (verse 3). From its first page Israel's calling is for the sake of the nations, and Paul calls this promise the gospel announced in advance (Galatians 3:8). Abram's first encounter with a foreign nation, which brings it plagues, shows how the bearer of the promise can obscure it.

When Abram's fear puts Sarai and the promise at risk, the LORD intervenes to protect them (verse 17). God's purposes do not depend on the faithfulness of the people he has chosen. Psalm 105:14-15 looks back on these travels and says God rebuked kings on the patriarchs' behalf.

At Bethel Abram builds an altar and ‘calls on the name of the LORD’ (verse 8), the phrase 4:26 used for the beginning of public worship. In a land held by others, his life is marked by worship addressed to God by name, a public declaration of whose land this is and whose protection he trusts.

words.note: Barakh, to bless. The verb occurs about 330 times in the Old Testament, more in Genesis and the Psalms than anywhere else, and its noun berakhah, blessing, about 70 times. Standard lexicons (BDB, HALOT) describe it as endowing with life, fruitfulness, and success, and also as declaring someone favored or, when people bless God, praising him. The root appears five times in verses 2 and 3. The last line can be read ‘all the families of the earth will be blessed through you’ or ‘will bless themselves by you’, that is, invoke your name in blessing; the text note explains why, and the Greek translation and the New Testament take the first sense.

Qalal, to be light or to treat lightly, translated curse in verse 3. It occurs about 80 times and ranges from ‘be trivial’ to ‘treat with contempt’ and ‘revile’. God uses two different verbs here: whoever treats Abram with contempt (qalal) God will curse (arar, the solemn word of 3:14 and 3:17, about 60 occurrences). In the Hebrew those who bless are plural and the one who despises is singular, which many commentators take to mean that blessing is expected to be the rule and contempt the exception.

Mishpachah, family or clan, about 300 times, most often in the tribal lists of Numbers and Joshua. It names the kinship group between the household and the tribe. Its use in verse 3 is pointed: the table of nations in Genesis 10 listed humanity by its mishpachot (10:5, 20, 31, 32), and now those same scattered families are the ones who will find blessing through Abram. The promise answers Babel family by family.

Shem, name, one of the commonest nouns in the Old Testament (about 860 times). A name stood for a person's reputation, identity, and lasting memory. At Babel the builders said ‘let us make a name for ourselves’ (11:4); here God says ‘I will make your name great’ (verse 2), a promise repeated to David (2 Samuel 7:9). In verse 8 the same word appears in the phrase ‘called on the name of the LORD’: Abram's name will be made great by God, and he in turn calls on God's name.

Gur, to sojourn, to live somewhere as a resident foreigner without the rights of a citizen (about 80 occurrences; the related noun ger, sojourner or stranger, about 90). Abram goes down to Egypt ‘to sojourn’ there (verse 10), and the patriarchs are called sojourners in Canaan itself (17:8, 23:4). Israel's later law repeatedly commands care for the ger because Israel had been strangers in Egypt (Exodus 22:21), and Hebrews 11:9 and 11:13 make the patriarchs' status as strangers a picture of the life of faith.

Zera, seed or offspring, about 230 times, a quarter of them in Genesis. In verse 7 God promises the land not to Abram himself but to his offspring, a promise that immediately raises a problem, since Sarai is barren (11:30). The word continues the thread that began with the woman's offspring in 3:15 and becomes the heart of the promises to Abraham. It is a collective singular, meaning descendants, and Paul builds an argument on its singular form in Galatians 3:16.

christ:
The New Testament treats this chapter as the first announcement of the gospel to the nations. Paul writes that “The Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, and foretold the gospel to Abraham” (Galatians 3:8), quoting the promise of verse 3, and he concludes that “those who have faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith” (Galatians 3:9). Christ, he says, redeemed us “in order that the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:14). In Galatians 3:16 he reads the singular word seed, promised the land in verse 7 and in later repetitions, as pointing to one offspring, Christ. Paul knows that zera normally means a whole line of descendants (he calls believers Abraham's seed in 3:29); his point is that the promise to the many is gathered up in the one.

Peter preached the same promise in the temple, reminding his hearers that God said to Abraham, “Through your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed” (Acts 3:25), and then announcing that God had raised up his Servant and sent him first to bless them. Matthew begins his Gospel by calling Jesus “the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1), and Mary's song and Zechariah's both celebrate God remembering his word to Abraham (Luke 1:54-55, 1:73). Jesus himself says that many will come from east and west to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Matthew 8:11), the families of the earth gathered at one table.

Hebrews holds up the moment of Abram's departure as a model of faith: he “obeyed and went, without knowing where he was going” (Hebrews 11:8), lived in tents as a stranger, and “was looking forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God” (Hebrews 11:10). Paul widens the land promise to the whole world: Abraham and his offspring would be ‘heir of the world’ (Romans 4:13). The promise of a place, first a strip of Canaan, becomes in the New Testament the hope of a renewed creation.

The second half of the chapter points to Christ by contrast rather than by pattern. Abram, the bearer of blessing, brings plagues on a nation, and the promise survives only because God protects it. Christian readers have seen here, as a theological reflection rather than a prediction, why the blessing of the nations would need a better offspring than Abram: one who would not save himself at another's expense, but give himself for others. The pattern of famine, descent to Egypt, deliverance, and departure also anticipates the exodus, which the Gospels in turn use to describe the saving work of Jesus; that link runs through the exodus and should not be pressed onto this episode directly.
interpretation:
Ancient Jewish retellings filled the silences of this chapter. Jubilees 12 has Abram burn the house of idols in Ur before the family leaves. The Genesis Apocryphon from Qumran (1QapGen, columns 19 and 20) gives Abram a warning dream of a cedar and a palm, praises Sarai's beauty at length, has her taken by ‘Pharaoh Zoan’, and keeps Pharaoh from touching her for two years by a plague until Abram prays and heals him. Philo of Alexandria's On the Migration of Abraham reads verses 1 to 6 as an allegory of the soul leaving the body, the senses, and speech to seek God. Josephus (Antiquities 1.154-168) presents Abram as the first to argue from the heavens that God is one, and says he taught the Egyptians arithmetic and astronomy.

The rabbis counted the call as the first of the ten trials of Abraham in Mishnah Avot 5:3 (Maimonides' list begins with it; Rashi's begins earlier with legends of Nimrod), with the binding of Isaac as the last. Genesis Rabbah 39:1 compares Abram to a traveler who sees a palace aglow (or ablaze) and asks whether it has no owner, until the owner looks out and says ‘I am the master’. Rashi reads lekh lekha as ‘go for your own good’. Nachmanides (Ramban) judged the descent to Egypt and the plan about Sarai a great sin, done unwittingly, and held that the later bondage in Egypt was decreed because of it. Abraham ibn Ezra noted that ‘the Canaanites were then in the land’ (verse 6) suggests a writer after their time and hinted at a ‘secret’; Spinoza's Theological-Political Treatise (1670) cited that comment in arguing that Moses did not write the whole Pentateuch.

Christian readers began with Hebrews 11:8-16. Augustine (City of God 16.19) defended Abram: Sarai was his sister by blood, so he concealed the truth without lying and entrusted her to God. The Reformers, Luther in his Lectures on Genesis (1535-1545) and Calvin in his commentary (1554), took the chapter as the pattern of faith that rests on a bare word of promise. Modern criticism, from Gunkel (1901) on, assigned 12:1-9 and 10-20 largely to the Yahwist source; Gerhard von Rad's commentary and Hans Walter Wolff's essay ‘The Kerygma of the Yahwist’ (Interpretation, 1966) made verses 1 to 3 the theological center of that source, the answer to the curse of chapters 3 to 11. J. Cheryl Exum's ‘Who's Afraid of the Endangered Ancestress?’ in Fragmented Women (1993) reads the wife-sister stories from Sarai's side, as tales about male fear that use a silent woman. Christopher J. H. Wright's The Mission of God (2006) made verses 1 to 3 the foundation of a biblical theology of mission.

In the synagogue the chapter opens the weekly portion Lekh Lekha (Genesis 12:1-17:27), read with Isaiah 40:27-41:16, which calls Israel ‘the descendant of Abraham My friend’ (Isaiah 41:8). The Revised Common Lectionary reads verses 1 to 4a on the Second Sunday in Lent in Year A, beside Romans 4 and John 3, and verses 1 to 9 at Proper 5 in Year A.
text:
English Bibles differ at a few points in this chapter, and one textual difference in the verses just before it affects how the call is dated.

In verse 1 the King James Version reads ‘the LORD had said’, placing the call back in Ur, in line with 15:7 and Stephen's words in Acts 7:2-4 (“The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was still in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran”). The Hebrew is the ordinary narrative form, and most modern versions read ‘said’. Stephen also says Abraham left Haran ‘after his father died’ (Acts 7:4). In the Masoretic Text, Terah was seventy when his sons were born (11:26) and died at 205 (11:32), so he would still have been alive when Abram left at seventy-five, unless Abram was a younger son born later. The Samaritan Pentateuch gives Terah's age at death as 145, which fits Stephen's statement, and some scholars think Stephen followed that textual tradition.

In verse 3 the verb translated ‘will be blessed’ is a Niphal, most naturally passive, as the Septuagint and the New Testament (Galatians 3:8, Acts 3:25) take it. When the promise returns in 22:18 and 26:4 the verb is a Hithpael, more naturally ‘will bless themselves’, and some translations (the RSV and NJPS, for example) render one or both forms that way; see the verse note. In verse 6 the King James Version reads ‘the plain of Moreh’, following the Aramaic Targum Onkelos, which rendered the word as a plain; the Septuagint has ‘the high oak’, and modern versions read ‘oak’, ‘terebinth’, or ‘great tree’. In verse 5 the King James Version's ‘the souls that they had gotten in Haran’ renders the Hebrew literally (‘the persons they had made’); modern versions interpret it as the people they had acquired. The Hebrew and English verse numbers are the same throughout the chapter.

teach.big: God answers the curse on a scattered world by calling one family to trust his promise and carry blessing to every family on earth, and he keeps that promise even when its bearer fails.

outline.t: God's call asks for everything (country, kindred, household) and promises more than it asks: a nation, a name, blessing, and blessing for all the families of the earth, the reversal of Babel.
Faith is shown by going: Abram obeys at seventy-five on nothing but God's word, and arrives in a land already occupied, a stranger in the place of promise.
God meets obedience with a clearer promise, and Abram answers with worship: tent for himself, altar for God, a public claim that the land is the LORD's.
The same man who trusted God with his future now trusts a scheme with his life; fear makes him plan his own safety at his wife's risk.
The plan works, and it costs Sarai everything: she is praised, taken, and silent, while Abram grows rich. Success is not the same as faithfulness.
God protects the promise and its mother, and a pagan king speaks the truth the man of God would not. God's faithfulness, not Abram's, carries the story.

teach.pitfalls:
The first misreading turns the call into a pattern of personal ambition: God has a great plan for your life, so step out and be blessed. The promise is not a general principle of success; it is God's particular answer to the world's curse, and its goal is the blessing of others. A related misuse applies verse 3 as a political rule, treating support for any modern state as automatically blessed and criticism as cursed. Christians hold different views about the modern state of Israel, but the verse speaks of Abram and his offspring as bearers of God's promise, and the New Testament reads that offspring in Christ (Galatians 3:16, 3:29); it should not be made into a slogan for any government.

A second misreading makes Abram a flawless hero. Verses 10 to 20 exist to show that he is not. Preachers sometimes excuse the lie as a half-truth or as prudence; the text lets Pharaoh rebuke Abram and gives Abram no reply, and the same scheme recurs in chapters 20 and 26. The opposite error treats the episode only as a morality tale about lying and misses its main point, which is God's protection of the promise. A third pitfall ignores Sarai. She is the one who pays for Abram's fear, and a sermon that hurries past her has not read the chapter.

Finally, avoid building doctrine on etymology, for example that Moreh means teacher and so the oak was a school of faith, or on the camels as proof or disproof of the whole story. Keep the weight where the text puts it: God's word, Abram's response, and God's faithfulness when that response fails.
teach.pastoral: This chapter will press on two kinds of people in the room. Some have left home, country, or family, as migrants, refugees, or people cut off for their faith, and the call of Abram and the law's care for the sojourner speak directly to them; God's people began as foreigners. Others have been used, like Sarai, by someone who should have protected them, and handed into danger for another's safety or gain. Teach the chapter so that they hear that God saw Sarai and acted for her, and that Scripture does not approve what Abram did. Do not tell a person in an abusive situation that submission to such a scheme is faithfulness; 1 Peter 3:6 commends Sarah for doing right and not giving way to fear, not for enduring harm. Make room, too, for those who recognize themselves in Abram: faith that fails under pressure is not the end of faith, and God did not abandon him.

hard.q: Why does Abram lie about Sarai, and why does Pharaoh suffer for it while Abram leaves rich?
hard.a:
The objection is sharp. Abram lies to save himself, Sarai is taken into a king's household, Pharaoh and his house are struck with plagues though he acted in ignorance, and Abram leaves Egypt with more than he brought. The story seems to reward deceit and punish the innocent. The medieval Jewish commentator Nachmanides already called Abram's conduct a great sin, both in endangering his wife and in leaving the land out of fear. Feminist readers such as J. Cheryl Exum (Fragmented Women, 1993) argue that the three wife-sister stories are told from a male point of view that treats the woman as property to be traded and never lets her speak, and skeptical readers ask what kind of God strikes the one person in the story who behaves honorably.

Interpreters have answered in several ways. Augustine (City of God 16.19) defended Abram: Sarai really was his sister (20:12), so he concealed the truth without lying and entrusted her to God, who kept her from harm. Many modern commentators reject that defense and read the narrator as judging Abram by the way he tells the story: Pharaoh, the outsider, asks three questions, and the man of promise has no answer; the wealth is listed without approval; and the same failure is shown recurring in Abram and in Isaac, like a family trait. On Pharaoh, many point out that the plagues are described as ‘because of Sarai’ (verse 17) and serve to protect her and reveal the truth, as they do in the parallel story (20:3-7), where God warns Abimelech in a dream before any harm is done. Others add that the king's taking of a foreign woman into his house was itself an act of power, whatever he knew of her marriage. Exum's reading has been welcomed by many for making Sarai visible, and questioned by others who think the narrator already shares her perspective by making her the one God acts for. Readers still differ on how far Abram is excused, but the text does not present his lie as a model.

hard.q: Was Abram a historical person, or a figure of later Israelite storytelling?
hard.a:
The skeptical case is serious. No text outside the Bible mentions Abram. Thomas L. Thompson (1974) and John Van Seters (1975) dismantled the confident mid-century case, associated with William F. Albright and his students, that the customs of Nuzi and Mari proved a second-millennium setting, showing that many parallels were misread or spread across a thousand years. Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman (The Bible Unearthed, 2001) point to details that seem to fit the first millennium better: camels as common beasts of burden, Philistines in Canaan (chapters 21 and 26), and ‘Ur of the Chaldeans’ (11:31), since the Chaldeans are known only from the first millennium. On this view the Abraham stories were shaped in the time of the monarchy or the exile, when Israel needed an ancestor who left Mesopotamia at God's call, and Ezekiel 33:24 shows exiles appealing to Abraham in exactly that way.

Others answer that absence of evidence is expected for a herdsman chief who left no inscriptions, and that the stories carry features hard to explain as late invention. Kenneth Kitchen (On the Reliability of the Old Testament, 2003) argues that the personal names of Abram's family, the names of towns around Haran, the treaty forms of the patriarchal covenants, and the movement of herders to Egypt fit the early second millennium. Many who hold this view treat names like ‘Ur of the Chaldeans’ and ‘Dan’ (14:14) as updates by later scribes for readers who knew the places by those names (the kind of later touch Ibn Ezra noticed in verse 6), and note that the camel evidence concerns when camels became common rather than whether any existed. A middle group, including many critical scholars, holds that the stories preserve old traditions of ancestors who moved between Mesopotamia and Canaan, but that their present form belongs to later centuries and history cannot confirm details. Christians who confess the reliability of Scripture hold different views on how the patriarchal narratives relate to history. What all agree on is that Israel understood its own existence as beginning with a call it did not deserve.

observe: List everything God promises in verses 1 to 3 and verse 7. Which promises concern Abram himself, and which look beyond him?
What does Abram say in verses 4 to 9, and what does he say in verses 10 to 20? What does Sarai say anywhere in the chapter?
Trace the events of verses 10 to 20 (famine, descent, plagues, sending away, possessions). Where does the same sequence appear later in the Bible?
interpret: How does the promise of a great name in verse 2 answer the builders of Babel in 11:4, and what does that say about how God deals with human ambition?
Why might Genesis place Abram's failure in Egypt immediately after his faithful obedience in verses 1 to 9?
Paul calls verse 3 ‘the gospel’ announced in advance (Galatians 3:8). In what sense is the blessing of all families the gospel?
apply: Abram left his country, family, and security on the strength of God's promise. What step of obedience are you facing where you cannot see the outcome?
God blesses Abram so that he will be a blessing to all families. How might your own blessings be meant for the sake of others?
The man who trusted God to leave home then trusted his own scheme in Egypt. Where are you tempted to protect yourself in ways that put others at risk?
